title: What are the strategies for API versioning, what are the tradeoffs, and how do you change a widely used API without breaking existing consumers?
shortTitle: What are the strategies for API versioning, what are the tradeoffs, and how do you change a widely used API without breaking existing consumers

s1_definition.profdef: API versioning is the discipline of evolving a published HTTP contract while allowing old and new consumers to coexist. The common strategies are URI path versioning such as `/v1/accounts`, query-parameter versioning such as `?version=2`, custom header versioning such as `Api-Version: 2`, and media-type (content negotiation) versioning such as `Accept: application/vnd.bank.v2+json`. The core principle for changing a widely used API without breakage is to make additive, backward-compatible changes within a version and to reserve a new version only for genuinely breaking changes, running the old and new versions in parallel through a deprecation window.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India prints account statement forms. Thousands of customers like Rajesh and Priya already know the current form. If the bank suddenly removes a column, everyone's software that reads the old form breaks. Instead, the bank adds a brand-new form labelled "Version 2", keeps printing the old "Version 1" for a while, tells everyone "Version 1 retires next year", and only then stops printing it. Adding an extra optional box to the old form is safe; removing or renaming a box is not, so that needs a new version.
s1_definition.oneliner: Version only for breaking changes, keep every change within a version additive and optional, run old and new in parallel, and deprecate before you delete.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** API versioning is the discipline of evolving a published HTTP contract while allowing old and new consumers to coexist. The common strategies are URI path versioning such as `/v1/accounts`, query-parameter versioning such as `?version=2`, custom header versioning such as `Api-Version: 2`, and media-type (content negotiation) versioning such as `Accept: application/vnd.bank.v2+json`. The core principle for changing a widely used API without breakage is to make additive, backward-compatible changes within a version and to reserve a new version only for genuinely breaking changes, running the old and new versions in parallel through a deprecation window.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India prints account statement forms. Thousands of customers like Rajesh and Priya already know the current form. If the bank suddenly removes a column, everyone's software that reads the old form breaks. Instead, the bank adds a brand-new form labelled "Version 2", keeps printing the old "Version 1" for a while, tells everyone "Version 1 retires next year", and only then stops printing it. Adding an extra optional box to the old form is safe; removing or renaming a box is not, so that needs a new version.

**One line to remember:** Version only for breaking changes, keep every change within a version additive and optional, run old and new in parallel, and deprecate before you delete.

sections.s2_technical:
The first thing to understand is what counts as a breaking change versus a safe change, because versioning strategy only matters once you know when you are forced to bump a version. A safe, backward-compatible change is one an existing consumer will not notice: adding a new optional field to a response, adding a new endpoint, adding a new optional request parameter with a sensible default, or accepting a new enum value the consumer can ignore. A breaking change forces existing consumers to update: removing or renaming a field, changing a field's type, making an optional field required, changing the meaning of an existing value, or changing an HTTP status code semantics. The golden rule is that you keep making additive changes within a version for as long as possible and only cut a new version when a change is genuinely breaking.

URI path versioning puts the version in the path, for example `GET /v1/accounts/SAV2001`. In Spring you simply map `@GetMapping("/v1/accounts/{id}")` and `@GetMapping("/v2/accounts/{id}")` on two methods. It is the most explicit and the easiest to route at a gateway, which is why it is the most common choice in banking APIs. The tradeoff is that the version is baked into the URL, so strictly a URL should identify a resource, not a representation, and purists dislike that, but in practice its clarity usually wins.

Query-parameter versioning uses `GET /accounts/SAV2001?version=2`. It keeps one URL per resource, but it is easy to forget, harder to cache cleanly, and clumsy to route at a gateway. Custom-header versioning uses something like `Api-Version: 2`, keeping URLs clean and treating the version as metadata, but it is invisible in a browser, harder to test with a plain link, and easy to omit. Media-type versioning uses content negotiation, `Accept: application/vnd.bank.v2+json`, which is the most RESTfully pure because the version describes the representation, but it is the most complex for clients and the least approachable for everyday use.

Whichever transport you pick, the real work is running versions in parallel safely. You keep `v1` controllers and `v2` controllers both live. Behind them you often share a service layer and map to version-specific DTOs, so a single piece of business logic serves both, with adapters translating between the internal model and each version's shape. You publish a deprecation policy: announce that `v1` is deprecated, return a `Deprecation` and `Sunset` HTTP header on `v1` responses so clients are warned programmatically, give consumers a concrete window such as six or twelve months, monitor who is still calling `v1`, and only remove it when traffic has drained. For truly widely used public APIs you never silently change behaviour; you add, deprecate, and remove on a schedule.

Senior nuances: prefer expand-and-contract (also called parallel change) even within a single version, where you add the new field, let clients migrate, then later remove the old one in a future version rather than at once. Use consumer-driven contract tests so you learn at build time if a change breaks a known consumer. Treat event schemas, like Kafka messages, with the same or stricter discipline because old events may be replayed long after the producer changed. And remember the cost of each live version is real: more code paths, more tests, more support, so you minimize the number of concurrent versions rather than spawning one per release.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's account API originally returned a customer's balance as a plain number of rupees. Later the bank went multi-currency and needed to return an amount plus a currency code. If they had simply changed the `balance` field's shape, every existing mobile app and partner integration reading the old number would have broken. This is exactly why a breaking change needs a new version: `v1` keeps the old plain-number shape, and `v2` returns a richer structured balance.

Problem 2 — The same API needed to start returning the account's branch code, which is brand new information. This is a safe, additive change: a new optional field can be added to the existing `v1` response because old clients simply ignore fields they do not know about, so no version bump is needed.

Problem 3 — The bank needed to retire `v1` eventually but could not do it overnight because partners integrate slowly. This is exactly the deprecation-window problem: `v1` must keep working while emitting `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers until traffic drains.

Our mini-project demonstrates URI path versioning with both versions live. The code defines an `Account` model, an `AccountService` shared by both versions, a `V1AccountController` returning the old flat shape with an added optional branch field, a `V2AccountController` returning the new structured multi-currency shape, and a demo that calls both and shows each returning correct data from the same underlying service, plus the deprecation headers on `v1`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/apiversion/ApiVersionDemo.java

# Run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.apiversion.ApiVersionDemo

# In a real Spring app, test both versions and see the deprecation headers:
curl -i http://localhost:8080/v1/accounts/SAV2001   # note Deprecation + Sunset headers
curl -i http://localhost:8080/v2/accounts/SAV2001   # structured balance
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one account in the internal store, Rajesh's SAV2001 with balance 1,000,000 INR and branch NBIN-MUM-001, and two clients, a legacy v1 client and a new v2 client, both asking for the same account.

Step 1: The v1 client calls the v1 controller. The controller asks the shared `AccountService` for the account. The service returns the full internal `Account` object, which contains everything including currency.

Step 2: The v1 controller maps that internal object into the old flat shape, copying the balance as a plain number so the legacy client sees exactly what it has always seen, and it additionally copies the branch code into a new optional field. Old clients that do not know about branch code simply ignore it, so this addition is safe.

Step 3: Because v1 is deprecated, the controller attaches `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers so the client is warned programmatically that this version retires on the advertised date, while still returning correct data today.

Step 4: The v2 client calls the v2 controller, which asks the very same service for the very same account. The business logic is not duplicated; only the shaping differs.

Step 5: The v2 controller maps the internal object into the new structured shape, turning the balance into an amount plus currency object. Both clients received correct data from one source of truth, and neither broke, which is the entire goal of versioning.

```
2026-10-24 14:40:02 WARNING V1 (DEPRECATED, Sunset=2027-06-30) → {id=SAV2001, name=Rajesh Kumar, balance=1000000.00, branch=NBIN-MUM-001}
2026-10-24 14:40:02 INFO    V2 → {id=SAV2001, name=Rajesh Kumar, balance=1000000.00 INR, branch=NBIN-MUM-001}
```

    │ GET /v1/accounts/SAV2001             │ GET /v2/accounts/SAV2001

    │ adds Deprecation + Sunset headers    │
    └───────────────┬──────────────────────┘

```

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Adapter: map internal Account → version-specific DTO shape   │
  │   WHY: one model, many representations, no logic duplication │

  │ O: new version = new controller + DTO, service unchanged      │
  │ L: both controllers honor the same resource contract          │
  │ D: controllers depend on AccountService abstraction           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐
  │ V1AccountController│◇────▶ │ AccountService    │
  │ + getAccount(id)  │        │ + findById(id)    │
  └──────────────────┘        └────────┬──────────┘
  ┌──────────────────┐                 │ returns
  │ V2AccountController│◇───────────────┘
  │ + getAccount(id)  │        ┌──────────────────┐
  └──────────────────┘        │ Account (internal)│
                              └──────────────────┘
  V1AccountResponse (flat balance)  V2AccountResponse (Money: amount+ccy)

  ── Change-Classification Decision ────────────────────────────
  Add optional field?        → SAFE → same version (v1 gets branchCode)
  Remove/rename/retype field? → BREAKING → new version (v2 Money shape)
  Behaviour/meaning change?   → BREAKING → new version + deprecate old

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. V1Controller.getAccount("SAV2001")
  2.   → AccountService.findById → Account
  3.   → map to flat V1 shape + add Deprecation/Sunset headers
  4. V2Controller.getAccount("SAV2001")
  5.   → AccountService.findById → Account (same source)
  6.   → map to structured V2 shape (Money)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
API versioning is how I evolve a published HTTP contract while letting old and new consumers coexist. I start by classifying the change, because that decides everything. A safe, backward-compatible change is one an existing consumer will not notice, like adding a new optional response field, a new endpoint, or a new optional request parameter with a default, and I make those freely within the current version because old clients simply ignore what they do not understand. A breaking change forces consumers to update, like removing or renaming a field, changing a field's type, making an optional field required, or changing the meaning of a value, and only those justify a new version.

For the transport I usually choose URI path versioning, like slash v1 slash accounts and slash v2 slash accounts, because it is the most explicit, the easiest to route at a gateway, and the clearest for consumers, which matters a lot for a bank with many partner integrations. The alternatives are query-parameter versioning, which is easy to forget and harder to cache, custom-header versioning, which keeps URLs clean but is invisible in a browser and easy to omit, and media-type content negotiation, which is the most RESTfully pure but the most complex for clients. Each has tradeoffs, and I pick based on who my consumers are and how they call me.

The real work is running versions in parallel safely. I keep the v1 and v2 controllers both live, but I share one service layer underneath and use adapters to map the single internal model into each version's DTO shape, so I never duplicate business logic. To retire a version I publish a deprecation policy: I announce that v1 is deprecated, I return Deprecation and Sunset headers so clients are warned programmatically, I give a concrete window of several months, I monitor who is still calling v1, and I remove it only after the traffic has drained. I never silently change behaviour on a widely used API.

On my project at National Bank of India the account API originally returned balance as a plain number, and when we went multi-currency we needed amount plus currency, which is a breaking change, so v1 kept the flat number while v2 returned a structured balance, both served by the same service. Adding the branch code, by contrast, was purely additive, so it went straight into v1 with no version bump. The lesson I always give is to prefer expand-and-contract, back changes with consumer-driven contract tests so breakage is caught at build time, treat event schemas like Kafka messages with equal or stricter care because they get replayed, and keep the number of live versions small because every live version is real cost in code, tests, and support.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I version only for breaking changes, keep every in-version change additive and optional, run old and new in parallel behind a shared service with adapters, and always deprecate with Sunset headers before I delete.
